# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi/

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Qoi](https://docs.rs/struct.Qoi.html)
- QOI descriptor value.
 This value is parsed from image header during decoding.
 Or provided by caller to drive encoding.
- [Var](https://docs.rs/struct.Var.html)
- Color variance value. Wrapping difference between two pixels.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Colors](https://docs.rs/enum.Colors.html)
- Image color space variants.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errros that may occur during image decoding.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that may occur during image encoding.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pixel](https://docs.rs/trait.Pixel.html)
- Trait for pixel types. Supports byte operations, channels accessing and modifying.

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi/0.6.1/rapid_qoi/

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

# rapid-qoi 0.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/latest

# rapid-qoi

Fast implementation of QOI format.
Reference implementation is here '[https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi](https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi)'

`rapid-qoi` is

-
no deps
-
no std
-
no unsafe
-
tiny
-
fast to build (0.8 sec clean build on i9)
-
one of the most efficient implementations of QOI encoder and decoder. `# Grand total for qoi benchmark suite # https://qoiformat.org/benchmark/qoi_benchmark_suite.tar decode ms encode ms decode mpps encode mpps ## Intel i9 qoi: 2.009 2.706 231.01 171.52 rapid_qoi: 1.404 2.520 330.72 184.23 ## Apple M1 qoi: 1.676 2.088 277.01 222.26 rapid_qoi: 1.100 1.836 421.99 252.77`See [benches](https://docs.rs/benches)for full reports.
 Run`cargo run --release -p bench -- [iterations] [path]`

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

that support `CheckedBitPattern`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.
- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroableInOption.html)- InOption
- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of.html)- of
- Re-interprets `&T`as`&[u8]`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of_mut.html)- of_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut T`as`&mut [u8]`.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast `A`into`B`
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_mut.html)- mut
- Cast `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_ref.html)- ref
- Cast `&A`into`&B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice.html)- slice
- Cast `&[A]`into`&[B]`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice_mut.html)- slice_ - mut
- Cast `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `slice`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html)- bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_mut.html)- bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast.html)- cast - `must_cast`
- Cast `A`into`B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref - `must_cast`
- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice - `must_cast`
- Convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to.html)- align_ - to
- As `align_to``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to_mut.html)- align_ - to_ - mut
- As `align_to_mut``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_read_unaligned.html)- read_ - unaligned
- Reads the slice into a `T`value.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast.html)- cast
- Try to cast `A`into`B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut
- Try to convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref
- Try to convert a `&A`into`&B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice
- Try to convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut
- Try to convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes_mut.html)- from_ - bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_pod_read_unaligned.html)- pod_ - read_ - unaligned
- Reads from the bytes as if they were a `T`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `target`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [zeroed](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroed.html)- `const_zeroed`
- Same as `Zeroable::zeroed``const fn`const.

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/latest/target-redirect/rapid_qoi/

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Qoi](https://docs.rs/struct.Qoi.html)
- QOI descriptor value.
 This value is parsed from image header during decoding.
 Or provided by caller to drive encoding.
- [Var](https://docs.rs/struct.Var.html)
- Color variance value. Wrapping difference between two pixels.

- Errors that may occur during image encoding.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

A2A protocol implementation for agent-to-agent communication with Model Context Protocol (MCP) server support.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Artifact and artifact collection types

# mongreldb_kit_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mongreldb-kit-core/0.9.0/mongreldb_kit_core/

## Expand description

Core, language-neutral model for MongrelDB Kit.

This crate contains the schema model, key encoding, validation, constraint
planning, migration planning, and query AST used by the storage-backed
`mongreldb-kit` crate and by language bindings.

# ggen_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ggen-core/26.7.2/ggen_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ggen-core---core-graph-aware-code-generation-engine)ggen-core - Core graph-aware code generation engine

This crate provides the core functionality for RDF-based code generation, including template processing, RDF handling, and deterministic output generation.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`ggen-core` is the foundational crate for the ggen code generation system. It provides:

- **Template Processing**: Parse, render, and generate code from templates with RDF integration
- **RDF Graph Management**: Load, query, and manipulate RDF data using SPARQL
- **Project Generation**: Scaffold complete projects from templates
- **Registry Integration**: Discover and install template packs from the registry
- **Lifecycle Management**: Orchestrate build, test, and deployment phases
- **Deterministic Output**: Ensure reproducible code generation

[§](https://docs.rs#key-modules)Key Modules

[§](https://docs.rs#template-system)Template System

- `template`
- `templates`
- `pipeline`
- `generator`

[§](https://docs.rs#rdf-integration)RDF Integration

- `graph`
- `rdf`
- `delta`

[§](https://docs.rs#project-management)Project Management

- `project_generator`
- `cli_generator`
- `lifecycle`

[§](https://docs.rs#registry-and-packs)Registry and Packs

- `registry`
- `cache`
- `lockfile`
- `resolver`
- `gpack`

[§](https://docs.rs#utilities)Utilities

- `inject`

- `preprocessor`
- `register`

[§](https://docs.rs#security-week-4-hardening)Security (Week 4 Hardening)

- `security`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-template-generation)Basic Template Generation

```
use crate::{Generator, GenContext, Pipeline};
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use std::path::PathBuf;
let pipeline = Pipeline::new()?;
let mut vars = BTreeMap::new();
vars.insert("name".to_string(), "MyApp".to_string());
let ctx = GenContext::new(
    PathBuf::from("template.tmpl"),
    PathBuf::from("output")
).with_vars(vars);
let mut generator = Generator::new(pipeline, ctx);
let output_path = generator.generate()?;
println!("Generated: {:?}", output_path);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-rdf-graph)Using RDF Graph

```
use ggen_core::Graph;
use oxigraph::sparql::QueryResults;
let graph = Graph::new()?;
graph.insert_turtle(r#"
    @prefix ex: <http://example.org/> .
    ex:alice a ex:Person ;
             ex:name "Alice" .
"#)?;
let results = graph.query("SELECT ?s ?o WHERE { ?s ex:name ?o }")?;
if let QueryResults::Solutions(solutions) = results {
    assert!(solutions.count() > 0);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#creating-a-new-project)Creating a New Project

```
use crate::project_generator::{ProjectConfig, ProjectType, create_new_project};
use std::path::PathBuf;
let config = ProjectConfig {
    name: "my-cli".to_string(),
    project_type: ProjectType::RustCli,
    framework: None,
    path: PathBuf::from("."),
};
create_new_project(&config).await?;
```

# tdsl_render - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tdsl-render/1.23.0/tdsl_render/

## Expand description

Timeline DSL renderer: `TimelineIr` → standalone HTML with inline SVG.

The public entry point is [ render_html](https://docs.rs/fn.render_html.html). Internally it:

- Computes a `layout::LayoutModel`
- Serializes it to an SVG string.
- Wraps the SVG in an HTML document with embedded CSS (hover tooltips only, no JS).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use layout::`- [GridStyle](https://docs.rs/layout/enum.GridStyle.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [LayoutModel](https://docs.rs/layout/struct.LayoutModel.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [LayoutStyle](https://docs.rs/layout/enum.LayoutStyle.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [Orientation](https://docs.rs/layout/enum.Orientation.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [RenderOptions](https://docs.rs/layout/struct.RenderOptions.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [Theme](https://docs.rs/layout/enum.Theme.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_html.html)- html
- Render the given IR as a standalone HTML document string.
- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_svg_only.html)- svg_ - only
- Render the given IR as a standalone SVG string.

# facett_icebergview - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-icebergview/0.1.10/facett_icebergview/

## Expand description

**facett-icebergview** — browse **and time-travel** one Iceberg table, drawn
from **Arrow  RecordBatches**. The component is

*engine-agnostic*: you hand it, per Iceberg snapshot, the snapshot’s metadata + its materialized Arrow frame; it renders a

**snapshot picker**(newest-first, showing snapshot id / timestamp / row-count) over a virtualized,

**paged**row grid (the rows come from

[, built from the batch via](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[). Selecting a snapshot loads](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)

`facett_arrow`*that*snapshot’s frame — time travel.

Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json`), so it drops into a `FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through
`facett_core::harness`: drive [/](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.select_snapshot)

`IcebergView::select_snapshot`[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.set_page)

`IcebergView::set_page``state_json` (the current snapshot, the snapshot list,
and the visible rows all change). `state_json` exposes:- `table`— the table name,
- `snapshots`— every snapshot newest-first (- `id`,- `timestamp_ms`,- `rows`),
- `current`— the selected snapshot id,
- `total_rows`/- `page`/- `page_size`/- `visible_rows`— the paged view.

**Why not just  facett-table?** A table viewer shows

*one*frame. This adds the Iceberg dimension — the history of snapshots and the control to scrub between them — which is the whole point of a lakehouse table browser. The adapter that

*fills*it from a real catalog (skade) lives host-side (korp / nornir) so this crate never takes a hard catalog/engine dependency.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iceberg](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html)- View
- A browse + time-travel viewer for one Iceberg table.
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.Snapshot.html)
- One snapshot paired with the Arrow frame that materializes it. The frame is a
`Vec<RecordBatch>`exactly as a scan returns it;`IcebergView`concatenates the rows into a paged`Table`
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.SnapshotMeta.html)- Meta
- One Iceberg snapshot’s identity, for the picker + `state_json`. Mirrors what`iceberg::spec::Snapshot`exposes (`snapshot_id()`/`timestamp_ms()`) plus a row count the host computes (scan count, or the snapshot summary’s`total-records`).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE.html)- PAGE_ - SIZE
- Default rows shown per page (the Table is virtualized, but paging keeps a huge
snapshot from being cell-formatted all at once and makes `visible_rows`meaningful for headless assertions).

# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`facett_core::FacetDeck`**Wall**mode (

[) so every pane (and thus several](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.wall_ui)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

`FacetDeck::ui`[§](https://docs.rs#engine-agnostic)Engine-agnostic

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host
(nornir’s viz) opens its Iceberg warehouse, reads each table, maps the rows to
a [ PaneData](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html) view-model, and hands them in. This crate never depends on
iceberg/skade/nornir.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-registry-table--view-kind)The registry (table → view-kind)

[ WarehouseRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html) maps a

**table name**to the

[it should render as, so adding a table is one](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)

`ViewKind``register(...)` line. The host queries the
registry to decide which [to build for a table; explicit join-panes (e.g. the call graph from](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)

`PaneData``call_edges`×`symbol_facts`) are added directly.[§](https://docs.rs#robot-testable)Robot-testable

[ WarehouseDeck](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html) is itself a

[, so it drops into nornir’s viz and is headless-assertable.](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`[exposes](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html#method.state_json)

`WarehouseDeck::state_json``pane_count`,
per-kind counts (`graph3d_count`, `grid_count`, …), and a `panes` array
carrying each pane’s `nodes`/`edges`/`rows`/`series`, plus the composed deck
state (whose `trace.ran` lists `deck.wall:<title>` for every pane that drew).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

---

# rapid-qoi 0.6.1 - Docs.rs

# rapid-qoi

Fast implementation of QOI format.
Reference implementation is here '[https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi](https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi)'

`rapid-qoi` is

-
no deps
-
no std
-
no unsafe
-
tiny
-
fast to build (0.8 sec clean build on i9)
-
one of the most efficient implementations of QOI encoder and decoder. `# Grand total for qoi benchmark suite # https://qoiformat.org/benchmark/qoi_benchmark_suite.tar decode ms encode ms decode mpps encode mpps ## Intel i9 qoi: 2.009 2.706 231.01 171.52 rapid_qoi: 1.404 2.520 330.72 184.23 ## Apple M1 qoi: 1.676 2.088 277.01 222.26 rapid_qoi: 1.100 1.836 421.99 252.77`See [benches](https://docs.rs/benches)for full reports.
 Run`cargo run --release -p bench -- [iterations] [path]`

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/0.6.1/target-redirect/rapid_qoi/

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Qoi](https://docs.rs/struct.Qoi.html)
- QOI descriptor value.
 This value is parsed from image header during decoding.
 Or provided by caller to drive encoding.
- [Var](https://docs.rs/struct.Var.html)
- Color variance value. Wrapping difference between two pixels.

- Errors that may occur during image encoding.
