# rapid_qoi/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! QOI - The "Quite OK Image" format for fast, lossless image compression
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! <https://phoboslab.org>
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! 20% better compression.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! # Data Format
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data "chunks" and an
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! 8-byte end marker.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```rust
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! #[repr(C)]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! struct QoiHeader {
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!     magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! }
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ```
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.\
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! Pixels are encoded as
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!  * a run of the previous pixel
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!  * an index into an array of previously seen pixels
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!  * a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!  * full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ("un-premultiplied alpha").
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! The hash function for the index is:
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! ```rust,ignore
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! index_position = (r * 3 + g * 5 + b * 7 + a * 11) % 64
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ```
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.\
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! presence of an 8-bit tag first.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! The byte stream's end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! The possible chunks are:
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ```text
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! .- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! |-------+-----------------|
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! |  0  0 |     index       |
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! `-------------------------`
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! 2-bit tag `0b00`\
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! 6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`\
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ```text
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! .- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! |-------+-----+-----+-----|
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! |  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! `-------------------------`
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! ```
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! 2-bit tag `0b01`\
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! 2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! 2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! 2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.\
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! `0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).\
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```text
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! .- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! |         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! |-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! |  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! `---------------------------------------------------`
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! 2-bit tag `0b10`\
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! 6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`\
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! 4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`\
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! 4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`\
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! ```rust,ignore
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.\
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.\
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```text
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! .- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! |-------+-----------------|
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! |  1  1 |       run       |
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! `-------------------------`
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! 2-bit tag `0b11`\
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! 6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`\
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! (`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! `QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! ```text
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! .- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! |         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! |-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! |  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! `-------------------------------------------------------`
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! 8-bit tag `0b11111110`\
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! 8-bit   red channel value\
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! 8-bit green channel value\
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! 8-bit  blue channel value\
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! ```text
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! .- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! |         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! |-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! |  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! `-----------------------------------------------------------------`
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ```
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! 8-bit tag `0b11111111`\
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! 8-bit   red channel value\
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! 8-bit green channel value\
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! 8-bit  blue channel value\
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! 8-bit alpha channel value
[147](https://docs.rs#147)#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)#![deny(missing_copy_implementations)]
[149](https://docs.rs#149)#![deny(missing_debug_implementations)]
[150](https://docs.rs#150)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)extern crate alloc;
[154](https://docs.rs#154)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)use core::{
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    convert::TryInto,
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    fmt::{self, Display},
[158](https://docs.rs#158)};
[159](https://docs.rs#159)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)mod decode;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)mod encode;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)pub use decode::DecodeError;
[164](https://docs.rs#164)pub use encode::EncodeError;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)const QOI_OP_INDEX: u8 = 0x00; /* 00xxxxxx */
[167](https://docs.rs#167)const QOI_OP_DIFF: u8 = 0x40; /* 01xxxxxx */
[168](https://docs.rs#168)const QOI_OP_LUMA: u8 = 0x80; /* 10xxxxxx */
[169](https://docs.rs#169)const QOI_OP_RUN: u8 = 0xc0; /* 11xxxxxx */
[170](https://docs.rs#170)const QOI_OP_RGB: u8 = 0xfe; /* 11111110 */
[171](https://docs.rs#171)const QOI_OP_RGBA: u8 = 0xff; /* 11111111 */
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)const QOI_MAGIC: u32 = u32::from_be_bytes(*b"qoif");
[174](https://docs.rs#174)const QOI_HEADER_SIZE: usize = 14;
[175](https://docs.rs#175)const QOI_PADDING: usize = 8;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// Trait for pixel types.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// Supports byte operations, channels accessing and modifying.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)pub trait Pixel: Copy + Eq {
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    fn new() -> Self;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    fn new_opaque() -> Self;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    fn read(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]);
[187](https://docs.rs#187)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    fn write(&self, bytes: &mut [u8]);
[189](https://docs.rs#189)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn rgb(&self) -> [u8; 3];
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    fn rgba(&self) -> [u8; 4];
[195](https://docs.rs#195)
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    fn r(&self) -> u8;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    fn g(&self) -> u8;
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    fn b(&self) -> u8;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    fn a(&self) -> u8;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn set_r(&mut self, r: u8);
[205](https://docs.rs#205)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    fn set_g(&mut self, g: u8);
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    fn set_b(&mut self, b: u8);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    fn set_a(&mut self, a: u8);
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    fn set_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8);
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    fn set_rgba(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8, a: u8);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn add_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8);
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    fn hash(&self) -> u8;
[219](https://docs.rs#219)}
[220](https://docs.rs#220)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)impl Pixel for [u8; 3] {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool = false;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    #[inline]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    fn new() -> Self {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        [0; 3]
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    #[inline]
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    fn new_opaque() -> Self {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        [0; 3]
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    #[inline]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    fn read(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        self.copy_from_slice(bytes);
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    #[inline]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    fn write(&self, bytes: &mut [u8]) {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        assert_eq!(bytes.len(), self.len());
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        bytes.copy_from_slice(self)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    #[inline]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var {
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        let r = self[0].wrapping_sub(prev[0]);
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let g = self[1].wrapping_sub(prev[1]);
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        let b = self[2].wrapping_sub(prev[2]);
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        Var { r, g, b }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    #[inline]
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    fn r(&self) -> u8 {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        self[0]
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    }
[258](https://docs.rs#258)
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    #[inline]
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    fn g(&self) -> u8 {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        self[1]
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    #[inline]
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    fn b(&self) -> u8 {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        self[2]
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    }
[268](https://docs.rs#268)
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    #[inline]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    fn rgb(&self) -> [u8; 3] {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        *self
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    #[inline]
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    fn rgba(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        unreachable!()
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    }
[278](https://docs.rs#278)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    #[inline]
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    fn a(&self) -> u8 {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        255
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    #[inline]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    fn set_r(&mut self, r: u8) {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        self[0] = r;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    #[inline]
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    fn set_g(&mut self, g: u8) {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        self[1] = g;
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    #[inline]
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    fn set_b(&mut self, b: u8) {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        self[2] = b;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    #[inline]
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    fn set_a(&mut self, a: u8) {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        debug_assert_eq!(a, 255);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    #[inline]
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    fn set_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        self[0] = r;
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        self[1] = g;
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        self[2] = b;
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    #[inline]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    fn set_rgba(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8, a: u8) {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        debug_assert_eq!(a, 255);
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        self[0] = r;
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        self[1] = g;
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        self[2] = b;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    #[inline]
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    fn add_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        self[0] = self[0].wrapping_add(r);
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        self[1] = self[1].wrapping_add(g);
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        self[2] = self[2].wrapping_add(b);
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    // #[inline]
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    // fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    //     let [r, g, b] = self;
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    //     r.wrapping_mul(3)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    //         .wrapping_add(g.wrapping_mul(5))
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    //         .wrapping_add(b.wrapping_mul(7).wrapping_add(245))
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    //         & 63
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    // }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    #[inline]
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)        let [r, g, b] = *self;
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        let v = u32::from_ne_bytes([r, g, b, 0xff]);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        let s = (((v as u64) << 32) | (v as u64)) & 0xFF00FF0000FF00FF;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        s.wrapping_mul(0x030007000005000Bu64.to_le()).swap_bytes() as u8 & 63
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    }
[344](https://docs.rs#344)}
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)// /// Four channel pixel type.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)// /// Typically channels are Red, Green, Blue and Alpha.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)// #[repr(transparent)]
[349](https://docs.rs#349)// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)// pub struct Rgba {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//     pub rgba: [u8; 4],
[352](https://docs.rs#352)// }
[353](https://docs.rs#353)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)impl Pixel for [u8; 4] {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool = true;
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    #[inline]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    fn new() -> Self {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        [0; 4]
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    }
[361](https://docs.rs#361)
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    #[inline]
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    fn new_opaque() -> Self {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        [0, 0, 0, 0xff]
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    #[inline]
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    fn read(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        match bytes.try_into() {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)            Ok(rgba) => {
[371](https://docs.rs#371)                *self = rgba;
[372](https://docs.rs#372)            }
[373](https://docs.rs#373)            _ => unreachable(),
[374](https://docs.rs#374)        }
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    }
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    #[inline]
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    fn write(&self, bytes: &mut [u8]) {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)        assert_eq!(bytes.len(), self.len());
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        bytes.copy_from_slice(self)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    #[inline]
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        let [r, g, b, a] = *self;
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        let [pr, pg, pb, pa] = *prev;
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        debug_assert_eq!(a, pa);
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        let r = r.wrapping_sub(pr);
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        let g = g.wrapping_sub(pg);
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        let b = b.wrapping_sub(pb);
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        Var { r, g, b }
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    #[inline]
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    fn r(&self) -> u8 {
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        self[0]
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    #[inline]
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    fn g(&self) -> u8 {
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        self[1]
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    }
[405](https://docs.rs#405)
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    #[inline]
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    fn b(&self) -> u8 {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        self[2]
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    }
[410](https://docs.rs#410)
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    #[inline]
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    fn rgb(&self) -> [u8; 3] {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        let [r, g, b, _] = *self;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)        [r, g, b]
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    }
[416](https://docs.rs#416)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    #[inline]
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    fn rgba(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        *self
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    }
[421](https://docs.rs#421)
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    #[inline]
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    fn a(&self) -> u8 {
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        self[3]
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    }
[426](https://docs.rs#426)
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    #[inline]
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    fn set_r(&mut self, r: u8) {
[429](https://docs.rs#429)        self[0] = r;
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    }
[431](https://docs.rs#431)
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    #[inline]

[458](https://docs.rs#458)    fn add_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) {
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        self[0] = self[0].wrapping_add(r);
[460](https://docs.rs#460)        self[1] = self[1].wrapping_add(g);
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        self[2] = self[2].wrapping_add(b);
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    }

[473](https://docs.rs#473)    #[inline]
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        let v = u32::from_ne_bytes(*self);
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        let s = (((v as u64) << 32) | (v as u64)) & 0xFF00FF0000FF00FF;
[477](https://docs.rs#477)
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        s.wrapping_mul(0x030007000005000Bu64.to_le()).swap_bytes() as u8 & 63
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    }
[480](https://docs.rs#480)}
[481](https://docs.rs#481)
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// Color variance value.
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// Wrapping difference between two pixels.
[484](https://docs.rs#484)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[485](https://docs.rs#485)#[repr(C)]
[486](https://docs.rs#486)pub struct Var {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    pub r: u8,
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    pub g: u8,
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    pub b: u8,
[490](https://docs.rs#490)}
[491](https://docs.rs#491)
[492](https://docs.rs#492)impl Var {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    #[inline]
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    fn diff(&self) -> Option<u8> {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        let r = self.r.wrapping_add(2);
[496](https://docs.rs#496)        let g = self.g.wrapping_add(2);
[497](https://docs.rs#497)        let b = self.b.wrapping_add(2);
[498](https://docs.rs#498)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        match r | g | b {
[500](https://docs.rs#500)            0x00..=0x03 => Some(QOI_OP_DIFF | (r << 4) as u8 | (g << 2) as u8 | b as u8),
[501](https://docs.rs#501)            _ => None,
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    }
[504](https://docs.rs#504)
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    #[inline]
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    fn luma(&self) -> Option<[u8; 2]> {
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        let r = self.r.wrapping_add(8).wrapping_sub(self.g);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        let g = self.g.wrapping_add(32);
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        let b = self.b.wrapping_add(8).wrapping_sub(self.g);
[510](https://docs.rs#510)
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        match (r | b, g) {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            (0x00..=0x0F, 0x00..=0x3F) => Some([QOI_OP_LUMA | g, r << 4 | b]),
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            _ => None,
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        }
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    }
[516](https://docs.rs#516)}

# Qoi in rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi/0.6.1/rapid_qoi/struct.Qoi.html

## Expand description

QOI descriptor value.

This value is parsed from image header during decoding.

Or provided by caller to drive encoding.

Decode a QOI image from bytes slice.

Decoded raw RGB or RGBA pixels are written into `output` slice.

On success this function returns `Ok(qoi)` with `qoi` describing image dimensions and color space.

On failure this function returns `Err(err)` with `err` describing cause of the error.

# DecodeError in rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi/0.6.1/rapid_qoi/enum.DecodeError.html

```
pub enum DecodeError {
    NotEnoughData,
    InvalidMagic,
    InvalidChannelsValue,
    InvalidColorSpaceValue,
    OutputIsTooSmall,
}
```
## Expand description

Errros that may occur during image decoding.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NotEnoughData)

### NotEnoughData

Buffer does not contain enough encoded data.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidMagic)

### InvalidMagic

Encoded header contains invalid magic value.

First four bytes must contain `b"qoif"`.

This usually indicates that buffer does not contain QOI image.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidChannelsValue)

### InvalidChannelsValue

Encoded header contains invalud channels number.

QOI supports only images with `3` or `4` channels.

Any other value cannot be produced by valid encoder.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidColorSpaceValue)

### InvalidColorSpaceValue

Encoded header contains invalud color space value.’
QOI supports only images with SRGB color channels and linear alpha (if present) denoted by `0` and all linear channels denoted by `1`.

Any other value cannot be produced by valid encoder.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.OutputIsTooSmall)

### OutputIsTooSmall

Output buffer is too small to fit decoded image.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rapid_qoi/decode.rs.html#54)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Error-for-DecodeError)### impl [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html) for [DecodeError](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)

Available on **crate feature **`std` only.

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Error-for-DecodeError)

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi/latest/rapid_qoi/

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Qoi](https://docs.rs/struct.Qoi.html)
- QOI descriptor value.
 This value is parsed from image header during decoding.
 Or provided by caller to drive encoding.
- [Var](https://docs.rs/struct.Var.html)
- Color variance value. Wrapping difference between two pixels.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Colors](https://docs.rs/enum.Colors.html)
- Image color space variants.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- Errros that may occur during image decoding.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that may occur during image encoding.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Pixel](https://docs.rs/trait.Pixel.html)
- Trait for pixel types. Supports byte operations, channels accessing and modifying.

# bytemuck 1.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytemuck/^1.0

# bytemuck

A crate for mucking around with piles of bytes.

This crate lets you safely perform "bit cast" operations between data types. That's where you take a value and just reinterpret the bits as being some other type of value, without changing the bits.

- This is **not**like the`as`keyword
- This is **not**like the`From`trait
- It is **most like**`f32::to_bits`

### Here's the part you're more likely to care about: *you can do this with slices too!*

When a slice is involved it's not a *direct* bitcast. Instead, the `cast_slice`
and `cast_slice_mut` functions will pull apart a slice's data and give you a new
slice that's the same span of memory just viewed as the new type. If the size of
the slice's element changes then the length of the slice you get back will be
changed accordingly.

This lets you cast a slice of color values into a slice of `u8` and send it to
the GPU, or things like that. I'm sure there's other examples, but honestly this
crate is as popular as it is mostly because of Rust's 3D graphics community
wanting to cast slices of different types into byte slices for sending to the
GPU. Hi friends! Push those vertices, or whatever it is that you all do.

## See Also

While `bytemuck` is full of unsafe code, I've also started a "sibling crate"
called [bitfrob](https://docs.rs/bitfrob/latest/bitfrob/), which is where
operations that are 100% safe will be added.

## Stability

- The crate is 1.0 and I consider this it to be "basically done". New features
are usually being accepted when other people want to put in the work, but
myself I wanna move on to using `bytemuck`in bigger projects.
- The default build of the `bytemuck`crate will continue to work with`rustc-1.34`for at least the rest of the`1.y.z`versions.
- Any other cargo features of the crate **are not**held to the same standard, and may work only on the latest Stable or even only on latest Nightly.

**Future Plans:** Once the [Safe Transmute Project](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2835-project-safe-transmute.html) completes and
stabilizes ("eventually") this crate will be updated to use that as the
underlying mechanism for transmutation bounds, and a 2.0 version of `bytemuck`
will be released. The hope is for the 1.0 to 2.0 transition to be as seamless as
possible, but the future is always uncertain.

---

# rapid-qoi

Fast implementation of QOI format.
Reference implementation is here '[https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi](https://github.com/phoboslab/qoi)'

`rapid-qoi` is

-
no deps
-
no std
-
no unsafe
-
tiny
-
fast to build (0.8 sec clean build on i9)
-
one of the most efficient implementations of QOI encoder and decoder. `# Grand total for qoi benchmark suite # https://qoiformat.org/benchmark/qoi_benchmark_suite.tar decode ms encode ms decode mpps encode mpps ## Intel i9 qoi: 2.009 2.706 231.01 171.52 rapid_qoi: 1.404 2.520 330.72 184.23 ## Apple M1 qoi: 1.676 2.088 277.01 222.26 rapid_qoi: 1.100 1.836 421.99 252.77`See [benches](https://docs.rs/benches)for full reports.

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rapid-qoi

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Qoi](https://docs.rs/struct.Qoi.html)
- QOI descriptor value.
 This value is parsed from image header during decoding.
 Or provided by caller to drive encoding.
- [Var](https://docs.rs/struct.Var.html)
- Color variance value. Wrapping difference between two pixels.

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error

- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors that may occur during image encoding.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- Trait for pixel types. Supports byte operations, channels accessing and modifying.

# bytemuck 1.25.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytemuck/1.25.0

# bytemuck

A crate for mucking around with piles of bytes.

This crate lets you safely perform "bit cast" operations between data types. That's where you take a value and just reinterpret the bits as being some other type of value, without changing the bits.

- This is **not**like the`as`keyword
- This is **not**like the`From`trait
- It is **most like**`f32::to_bits`

### Here's the part you're more likely to care about: *you can do this with slices too!*

When a slice is involved it's not a *direct* bitcast. Instead, the `cast_slice`
and `cast_slice_mut` functions will pull apart a slice's data and give you a new
slice that's the same span of memory just viewed as the new type. If the size of
the slice's element changes then the length of the slice you get back will be
changed accordingly.

This lets you cast a slice of color values into a slice of `u8` and send it to
the GPU, or things like that. I'm sure there's other examples, but honestly this
crate is as popular as it is mostly because of Rust's 3D graphics community
wanting to cast slices of different types into byte slices for sending to the
GPU. Hi friends! Push those vertices, or whatever it is that you all do.

## See Also

While `bytemuck` is full of unsafe code, I've also started a "sibling crate"
called [bitfrob](https://docs.rs/bitfrob/latest/bitfrob/), which is where
operations that are 100% safe will be added.

## Stability

- The crate is 1.0 and I consider this it to be "basically done". New features
are usually being accepted when other people want to put in the work, but
myself I wanna move on to using `bytemuck`in bigger projects.
- The default build of the `bytemuck`crate will continue to work with`rustc-1.34`for at least the rest of the`1.y.z`versions.
- Any other cargo features of the crate **are not**held to the same standard, and may work only on the latest Stable or even only on latest Nightly.

**Future Plans:** Once the [Safe Transmute Project](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2835-project-safe-transmute.html) completes and
stabilizes ("eventually") this crate will be updated to use that as the
underlying mechanism for transmutation bounds, and a 2.0 version of `bytemuck`
will be released. The hope is for the 1.0 to 2.0 transition to be as seamless as
possible, but the future is always uncertain.

---

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1.0.22/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```

---

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytemuck/1.25.0/target-redirect/bytemuck/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use checked::`- [CheckedBitPattern](https://docs.rs/checked/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html);
- `pub use`- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)::*;- `extern_crate_alloc`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [allocation](https://docs.rs/allocation/index.html)- `extern_crate_alloc`
- Stuff to boost things in the `alloc`crate.
- [checked](https://docs.rs/checked/index.html)
- Checked versions of the casting functions exposed in crate root
that support `CheckedBitPattern`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [offset_](https://docs.rs/macro.offset_of.html)- of
- Find the offset in bytes of the given `$field`of`$Type`. Requires an already initialized`$instance`value to work with.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [PodCast](https://docs.rs/enum.PodCastError.html)- Error
- The things that can go wrong when casting between `Pod`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.
- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroableInOption.html)- InOption
- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of.html)- of
- Re-interprets `&T`as`&[u8]`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of_mut.html)- of_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut T`as`&mut [u8]`.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast `A`into`B`
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_mut.html)- mut
- Cast `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_ref.html)- ref
- Cast `&A`into`&B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice.html)- slice
- Cast `&[A]`into`&[B]`.

- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.

- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref - `must_cast`
- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.

# NoUninit in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.NoUninit.html

## Expand description

Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.

The requirements for this is very similar to [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html),
except that it doesn’t require that all bit patterns of the type are valid,
i.e. it does not require the type to be

[. This limits what you can do with a type of this kind, but also broadens the included types to things like C-style enums. Notably, you can only cast from](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`*immutable*references to a

[type into](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)

`NoUninit`*immutable*references of any other type, no casting of mutable references or mutable references to slices etc.

[ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) is a subset of

[, meaning that any](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)

`NoUninit``T: Pod` is also
[but any](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)

`NoUninit``T: NoUninit` is not necessarily [. If possible, prefer implementing](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)

`Pod`[directly. To get more](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)

`Pod`[-like functionality for a type that is only](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)

`Pod`[, consider also implementing](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)

`NoUninit`[.](https://docs.rs/checked/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html)

`CheckedBitPattern`The rules for padding for various types and representations are documented
in the Rust reference section on [type layout](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#derive)Derive

A `#[derive(NoUninit)]` macro is provided under the `derive` feature flag
which will automatically validate the requirements of this trait and
implement the trait for you for both enums and structs. This is the
recommended method for implementing the trait, however it’s also possible to
do manually. If you implement it manually, you *must* carefully follow the
below safety rules.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The same as [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) except we disregard the rule about it must
allow any bit pattern (i.e. it does not need to be

[). Still, this is a quite strong guarantee about a type, so](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`*be careful*whem implementing it manually.

- The type must be inhabited (eg: no
[Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html)).
- The type must not contain any uninit (or padding) bytes, either in the
middle or on the end (eg: no `#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u8, u16)`, which has padding in the middle, and also no`#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u16, u8)`, which has padding on the end).
- Structs need to have all fields also be `NoUninit`.
- Structs need to be `repr(C)`or`repr(transparent)`. In the case of`repr(C)`, the`packed`and`align`repr modifiers can be used as long as all other rules end up being followed.
- Enums need to be `#[repr(Int)]`,`#[repr(C)]`, or both.
- Enums may have fields. If the enum has fields,
- Each variant’s fields must individually follow the same rules as a struct
- All variants must be the same size, and require no padding-to-alignment
- There must be no padding needed between the discriminant type and the “fields struct” of any variant

- It is disallowed for types to contain pointer types, `Cell`,`UnsafeCell`, atomics, and any other forms of interior mutability.
- More precisely: A shared reference to the type must allow reads, and
*only*reads. RustBelt’s separation logic is based on the notion that a type is allowed to define a sharing predicate, its own invariant that must hold for shared references, and this predicate is the reasoning that allow it to deal with atomic and cells etc. We require the sharing predicate to be trivial and permit only read-only access.
- There’s probably more, don’t mess it up (I mean it).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# AnyBitPattern in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.AnyBitPattern.html

## Expand description

Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.

The requirements for this is very similar to [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html), except that the type
can allow uninit (or padding) bytes. This limits what you can do with a type
of this kind, but also broadens the included types to

`repr(C)` `struct`s
that contain padding as well as `union`s. Notably, you can only cast
*immutable*references and

*owned*values into

[types, not](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`*mutable*references.

[ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) is a subset of

[, meaning that any](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern``T: Pod` is also
[but any](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern``T: AnyBitPattern` is not necessarily [.](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)

`Pod`[ AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html) is a subset of

[, meaning that any](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable``T: AnyBitPattern` is also [, but any](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable``T: Zeroable` is not
necessarily

`AnyBitPattern`[§](https://docs.rs#derive)Derive

A `#[derive(AnyBitPattern)]` macro is provided under the `derive` feature
flag which will automatically validate the requirements of this trait and
implement the trait for you for both structs and enums. This is the
recommended method for implementing the trait, however it’s also possible to
do manually. If you implement it manually, you *must* carefully follow the
below safety rules.

- *NOTE: even `C-style`, fieldless enums are intentionally**excluded**from this trait, since it is**unsound**for an enum to have a discriminant value that is not one of its defined variants.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Similar to [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) except we disregard the rule about it must not contain
uninit bytes. Still, this is a quite strong guarantee about a type, so

*be careful*when implementing it manually.

- The type must be inhabited (eg: no
[Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html)).
- The type must be valid for any bit pattern of its backing memory.
- Structs need to have all fields also be `AnyBitPattern`.
- It is disallowed for types to contain pointer types, `Cell`,`UnsafeCell`, atomics, and any other forms of interior mutability.
- More precisely: A shared reference to the type must allow reads, and
*only*reads. RustBelt’s separation logic is based on the notion that a type is allowed to define a sharing predicate, its own invariant that must hold for shared references, and this predicate is the reasoning that allow it to deal with atomic and cells etc. We require the sharing predicate to be trivial and permit only read-only access.
- There’s probably more, don’t mess it up (I mean it).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Pod in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.Pod.html

## Expand description

Marker trait for “plain old data”.

The point of this trait is that once something is marked “plain old data” you can really go to town with the bit fiddling and bit casting. Therefore, it’s a relatively strong claim to make about a type. Do not add this to your type casually.

**Reminder:** The results of casting around bytes between data types are
*endian dependant*. Little-endian machines are the most common, but
big-endian machines do exist (and big-endian is also used for “network
order” bytes).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The type must be inhabited (eg: no
[Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html)).
- The type must allow any bit pattern (eg: no `bool`or`char`, which have illegal bit patterns).
- The type must not contain any uninit (or padding) bytes, either in the
middle or on the end (eg: no `#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u8, u16)`, which has padding in the middle, and also no`#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u16, u8)`, which has padding on the end).
- The type needs to have all fields also be `Pod`.
- The type needs to be `repr(C)`or`repr(transparent)`. In the case of`repr(C)`, the`packed`and`align`repr modifiers can be used as long as all other rules end up being followed.
- It is disallowed for types to contain pointer types, `Cell`,`UnsafeCell`, atomics, and any other forms of interior mutability.
- More precisely: A shared reference to the type must allow reads, and
*only*reads. RustBelt’s separation logic is based on the notion that a type is allowed to define a sharing predicate, its own invariant that must hold for shared references, and this predicate is the reasoning that allow it to deal with atomic and cells etc. We require the sharing predicate to be trivial and permit only read-only access.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/pod.rs.html#39)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Pod-for-())

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/pod.rs.html#83)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Pod-for-PhantomPinned)

### impl [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) for [PhantomPinned](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/struct.PhantomPinned.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/pod.rs.html#138-144)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Pod-for-__m128)

**x86-64**only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/pod.rs.html#138-144)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Pod-for-__m256)

**x86-64**only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/pod.rs.html#178-183)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Pod-for-__m512)

# Zeroable in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.Zeroable.html

## Expand description

Trait for types that can be safely created with
[ zeroed](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/fn.zeroed.html).

An all-zeroes value may or may not be the same value as the
[Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) value of the type.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- Your type must be inhabited (eg: no
[Infallible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/enum.Infallible.html)).
- Your type must be allowed to be an “all zeroes” bit pattern (eg: no
`NonNull<T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Some `impl`s are feature gated due to the MSRV policy:

- `MaybeUninit<T>`was not available in 1.34.0, but is available under the- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`feature flag.
- `Atomic*`types require Rust 1.60.0 or later to work on certain platforms, but is available under the- `zeroable_atomics`feature flag.
- `[T; N]`for arbitrary- `N`requires the- `min_const_generics`feature flag.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# pack1 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pack1

## Expand description

Byte array newtypes for different primitive types.

Because they’re newtypes of byte arrays, they always have alignment 1.

Each type has `new` and `get` functions, as well as [ From](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html) impls. The

`new` and `get` functions are `const fn` with int types, but not yet with
floating types.The intended usage of this crate is that you can use these these types in a
`repr(C)` struct, along with manual padding, and then have each field at the
exact byte offset you desire (and with the necessary endian-ness), without
the normal `repr(packed)` problem that it interferes with references.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# offset_of in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/macro.offset_of.html

```
macro_rules! offset_of {
    ($instance:expr, $Type:path, $field:tt) => { ... };
    ($Type:path, $field:tt) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Find the offset in bytes of the given `$field` of `$Type`. Requires an
already initialized `$instance` value to work with.

This is similar to the macro from [ memoffset](https://docs.rs/memoffset),
however it uses no

`unsafe` code.This macro has a 3-argument and 2-argument version.

- In the 3-arg version you specify an instance of the type, the type itself, and the field name.
- In the 2-arg version the macro will call the `default`

The output of this macro is the byte offset of the field (as a `usize`). The
calculations of the macro are fixed across the entire program, but if the
type used is `repr(Rust)` then they’re *not* fixed across compilations or
compilers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#3-arg-usage)3-arg Usage

```
// enums can't derive default, and for this example we don't pick one
enum MyExampleEnum {
  A,
  B,
  C,
}
// so now our struct here doesn't have Default
#[repr(C)]
struct MyNotDefaultType {
  pub counter: i32,
  pub some_field: MyExampleEnum,
}
// but we provide an instance of the type and it's all good.
let val = MyNotDefaultType { counter: 5, some_field: MyExampleEnum::A };
assert_eq!(offset_of!(val, MyNotDefaultType, some_field), 4);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#2-arg-usage)2-arg Usage

```
#[derive(Default)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Vertex {
  pub loc: [f32; 3],
  pub color: [f32; 3],
}
// if the type impls Default the macro can make its own default instance.
assert_eq!(offset_of!(Vertex, loc), 0);
assert_eq!(offset_of!(Vertex, color), 12);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage-with-reprpacked-structs)Usage with `#[repr(packed)]` structs

Attempting to compute the offset of a `#[repr(packed)]` struct with
`bytemuck::offset_of!` requires an `unsafe` block. We hope to relax this in
the future, but currently it is required to work around a soundness hole in
Rust (See [rust-lang/rust#27060](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27060)).

**Warning:** This is only true for versions of bytemuck >
1.4.0. Previous versions of
`bytemuck::offset_of!`
will only emit a warning when used on the field of a packed struct in safe
code, which can lead to unsoundness.

For example, the following will fail to compile:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[repr(C, packed)]
#[derive(Default)]
struct Example {
  field: u32,
}
// Doesn't compile:
let _offset = bytemuck::offset_of!(Example, field);
```
While the error message this generates will mention the
`safe_packed_borrows` lint, the macro will still fail to compile even if
that lint is `#[allow]`ed:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Still doesn't compile:
#[allow(safe_packed_borrows)]
{
  let _offset = bytemuck::offset_of!(Example, field);
}
```
This *can* be worked around by using `unsafe`, but it is only sound to do so
if you can guarantee that taking a reference to the field is sound.

In practice, this means it only works for fields of align(1) types, or if
you know the field’s offset in advance (defeating the point of `offset_of`)
and can prove that the struct’s alignment and the field’s offset are enough
to prove the field’s alignment.

Once the `raw_ref` macros are available, a future version of this crate will
use them to lift the limitations of packed structs. For the duration of the
`1.x` version of this crate that will be behind an on-by-default cargo
feature (to maintain minimum rust version support).

---

# PodCastError in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/enum.PodCastError.html

```
pub enum PodCastError {
    TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned,
    OutputSliceWouldHaveSlop,
    SizeMismatch,
    AlignmentMismatch,
}
```
## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned)

### TargetAlignmentGreaterAndInputNotAligned

You tried to cast a reference into a reference to a type with a higher alignment requirement but the input reference wasn’t aligned.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.OutputSliceWouldHaveSlop)

### OutputSliceWouldHaveSlop

If the element size of a slice changes, then the output slice changes length accordingly. If the output slice wouldn’t be a whole number of elements, then the conversion fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SizeMismatch)

### SizeMismatch

When casting an individual `T`, `&T`, or `&mut T` value the
source size and destination size must be an exact match.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AlignmentMismatch)

### AlignmentMismatch

For this type of cast the alignments must be exactly the same and they were not so now you’re sad.

This error is generated **only** by operations that cast allocated types
(such as `Box` and `Vec`), because in that case the alignment must stay
exact.
