# Contiguous in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.Contiguous.html

`pub unsafe trait Contiguous: `[Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) + 'static {
    type [Int](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Int): [Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) + [Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html);
    const [MAX_VALUE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.MAX_VALUE): Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int);
    const [MIN_VALUE](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.MIN_VALUE): Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int);
    // Provided methods
    fn [from_integer](https://docs.rs#method.from_integer)(value: Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self> { ... }
[into_integer](https://docs.rs#method.into_integer)(self) -> Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait indicating that:

- A type has an equivalent representation to some known integral type.
- All instances of this type fall in a fixed range of values.
- Within that range, there are no gaps.

This is generally useful for fieldless enums (aka “c-style” enums), however
it’s important that it only be used for those with an explicit `#[repr]`, as
`#[repr(Rust)]` fieldess enums have an unspecified layout.

Additionally, you shouldn’t assume that all implementations are enums. Any type which meets the requirements above while following the rules under “Safety” below is valid.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[repr(u8)]
#[derive(Debug, Copy, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Foo {
  A = 0,
  B = 1,
  C = 2,
  D = 3,
  E = 4,
}
unsafe impl Contiguous for Foo {
  type Int = u8;
  const MIN_VALUE: u8 = Foo::A as u8;
  const MAX_VALUE: u8 = Foo::E as u8;
}
assert_eq!(Foo::from_integer(3).unwrap(), Foo::D);
assert_eq!(Foo::from_integer(8), None);
assert_eq!(Foo::C.into_integer(), 2);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This is an unsafe trait, and incorrectly implementing it is undefined behavior.

Informally, by implementing it, you’re asserting that `C` is identical to
the integral type `C::Int`, and that every `C` falls between `C::MIN_VALUE`
and `C::MAX_VALUE` exactly once, without any gaps.

Precisely, the guarantees you must uphold when implementing `Contiguous` for
some type `C` are:

-
The size of `C`and`C::Int`must be the same, and neither may be a ZST. (Note: alignment is explicitly allowed to differ)
-
`C::Int`must be a primitive integer, and not a wrapper type. In the future, this may be lifted to include cases where the behavior is identical for a relevant set of traits (Ord, arithmetic, …).
-
All `C::Int`s which are in the*inclusive*range between`C::MIN_VALUE`and`C::MAX_VALUE`are bitwise identical to unique valid instances of`C`.
-
There exist no instances of `C`such that their bitpatterns, when interpreted as instances of`C::Int`, fall outside of the`MAX_VALUE`/`MIN_VALUE`range – It is legal for unsafe code to assume that if it gets a`C`that implements`Contiguous`, it is in the appropriate range.
-
Finally, you promise not to provide overridden implementations of `Contiguous::from_integer`and`Contiguous::into_integer`.

For clarity, the following rules could be derived from the above, but are listed explicitly:

-
`C::MAX_VALUE`must be greater or equal to`C::MIN_VALUE`(therefore,`C`must be an inhabited type).
-
There exist no two values between `MIN_VALUE`and`MAX_VALUE`such that when interpreted as a`C`they are considered identical (by, say, match).

## Required Associated Constants[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-consts)

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

The primitive integer type with an identical representation to this type.

Contiguous is broadly intended for use with fieldless enums, and for
these the correct integer type is easy: The enum should have a
`#[repr(Int)]` or `#[repr(C)]` attribute, (if it does not, it is
*unsound* to implement `Contiguous`!).

-
For `#[repr(Int)]`, use the listed`Int`. e.g.`#[repr(u8)]`should use`type Int = u8`.
-
For `#[repr(C)]`, use whichever type the C compiler will use to represent the given enum. This is usually`c_int`(from`std::os::raw`or`libc`), but it’s up to you to make the determination as the implementer of the unsafe trait.

For precise rules, see the list under “Safety” above.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/contiguous.rs.html#122-139)#### fn [from_integer](https://docs.rs#method.from_integer)(value: Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/contiguous.rs.html#122-139)

#### fn [from_integer](https://docs.rs#method.from_integer)(value: Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self>

If `value` is within the range for valid instances of this type,
returns `Some(converted_value)`, otherwise, returns `None`.

This is a trait method so that you can write `value.into_integer()` in
your code. It is a contract of this trait that if you implement
`Contiguous` on your type you **must not** override this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

We will not panic for any correct implementation of `Contiguous`, but
*may* panic if we detect an incorrect one.

This is undefined behavior regardless, so it could have been the nasal demons at that point anyway ;).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/contiguous.rs.html#158-170)#### fn [into_integer](https://docs.rs#method.into_integer)(self) -> Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bytemuck/contiguous.rs.html#158-170)

#### fn [into_integer](https://docs.rs#method.into_integer)(self) -> Self::[Int](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html#associatedtype.Int)

Perform the conversion from `C` into the underlying integral type. This
mostly exists otherwise generic code would need unsafe for the `value as integer`

This is a trait method so that you can write `value.into_integer()` in
your code. It is a contract of this trait that if you implement
`Contiguous` on your type you **must not** override this method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

*may* panic if we detect an incorrect one.

This is undefined behavior regardless, so it could have been the nasal demons at that point anyway ;).

# TransparentWrapper in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/trait.TransparentWrapper.html

`pub unsafe trait TransparentWrapper<Inner: ?`[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)> {
    // Provided methods
    fn [wrap](https://docs.rs#method.wrap)(s: Inner) -> Self
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[wrap_ref](https://docs.rs#method.wrap_ref)(s: [&Inner](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> &Self { ... }
[wrap_mut](https://docs.rs#method.wrap_mut)(s: [&mut Inner](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> &mut Self { ... }
[wrap_slice](https://docs.rs#method.wrap_slice)(s: &[[Inner]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)) -> &[Self]
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[wrap_slice_mut](https://docs.rs#method.wrap_slice_mut)(s: &mut [[Inner]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)) -> &mut [Self]
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[peel](https://docs.rs#method.peel)(s: Self) -> Inner
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[peel_ref](https://docs.rs#method.peel_ref)(s: &Self) -> [&Inner](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html) { ... }
[peel_mut](https://docs.rs#method.peel_mut)(s: &mut Self) -> [&mut Inner](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html) { ... }
[peel_slice](https://docs.rs#method.peel_slice)(s: &[Self]) -> &[[Inner]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[peel_slice_mut](https://docs.rs#method.peel_slice_mut)(s: &mut [Self]) -> &mut [[Inner]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)
       where Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html),
             Inner: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]` wrapper
around the `Inner` value.

This allows safely copy transmuting between the `Inner` type and the
`TransparentWrapper` type. Functions like `wrap_{}` convert from the inner
type to the wrapper type and `peel_{}` functions do the inverse conversion
from the wrapper type to the inner type. We deliberately do not call the
wrapper-removing methods “unwrap” because at this point that word is too
strongly tied to the Option/ Result methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The safety contract of `TransparentWrapper` is relatively simple:

For a given `Wrapper` which implements `TransparentWrapper<Inner>`:

-
`Wrapper`must be a wrapper around`Inner`with an identical data representations. This either means that it must be a`#[repr(transparent)]`struct which contains a either a field of type`Inner`(or a field of some other transparent wrapper for`Inner`) as the only non-ZST field.
-
Any fields *other*than the`Inner`field must be trivially constructable ZSTs, for example`PhantomData`,`PhantomPinned`, etc. (When deriving`TransparentWrapper`on a type with ZST fields, the ZST fields must be`Zeroable`
-
The `Wrapper`may not impose additional alignment requirements over`Inner`.- Note: this is currently guaranteed by `repr(transparent)`, but there have been discussions of lifting it, so it’s stated here explicitly.

- Note: this is currently guaranteed by
-
All functions on `TransparentWrapper`**may not**be overridden.

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

If the wrapper imposes additional constraints upon the inner type which are
required for safety, it’s responsible for ensuring those still hold – this
generally requires preventing access to instances of the inner type, as
implementing `TransparentWrapper<U> for T` means anybody can call
`T::cast_ref(any_instance_of_u)`.

For example, it would be invalid to implement TransparentWrapper for `str`
to implement `TransparentWrapper` around `[u8]` because of this.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#basic)Basic

```
use bytemuck::TransparentWrapper;
#[repr(transparent)]
struct MyWrapper(SomeStruct);
unsafe impl TransparentWrapper<SomeStruct> for MyWrapper {}
// interpret a reference to &SomeStruct as a &MyWrapper
let thing = SomeStruct::default();
let inner_ref: &MyWrapper = MyWrapper::wrap_ref(&thing);
// Works with &mut too.
let mut mut_thing = SomeStruct::default();
let inner_mut: &mut MyWrapper = MyWrapper::wrap_mut(&mut mut_thing);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-dynamically-sized-types)Use with dynamically sized types

```
use bytemuck::TransparentWrapper;
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Slice<T>([T]);
unsafe impl<T> TransparentWrapper<[T]> for Slice<T> {}
let s = Slice::wrap_ref(&[1u32, 2, 3]);
assert_eq!(&s.0, &[1, 2, 3]);
let mut buf = [1, 2, 3u8];
let sm = Slice::wrap_mut(&mut buf);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#deriving)Deriving

When deriving, the non-wrapped fields must uphold all the normal
requirements, and must also be `Zeroable`.

```
use bytemuck::TransparentWrapper;
use std::marker::PhantomData;
#[derive(TransparentWrapper)]
#[repr(transparent)]
#[transparent(usize)]
struct Wrapper<T: ?Sized>(usize, PhantomData<T>); // PhantomData<T> implements Zeroable for all T
```
Here, an error will occur, because `MyZst` does not implement `Zeroable`.

# bytes_of in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.bytes_of.html

## Expand description

Re-interprets `&T` as `&[u8]`.

Any ZST becomes an empty slice, and in that case the pointer value of that empty slice might not match the pointer value of the input reference.

---

# bytes_of_mut in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.bytes_of_mut.html

`pub fn bytes_of_mut<T: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) + [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(t: [&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)] [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)## Expand description

Re-interprets `&mut T` as `&mut [u8]`.

Any ZST becomes an empty slice, and in that case the pointer value of that empty slice might not match the pointer value of the input reference.

# fill_zeroes in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.fill_zeroes.html

## Expand description

Fill all bytes of `slice` with zeroes (see [ Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)).

This is similar to `slice.fill(Zeroable::zeroed())`, but guarantees that any
padding bytes in `slice` are zeroed as well.

See also [ write_zeroes](https://docs.rs/fn.write_zeroes.html), which zeroes all bytes of a single value rather
than a slice.

---

# must_cast in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.must_cast.html

`pub const fn must_cast<A: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html), B: [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(a: A) -> B**crate feature**only.

`must_cast`## Expand description

Cast `A` into `B` if infalliable, or fail to compile.

Note that for this particular type of cast, alignment isn’t a factor. The input value is semantically copied into the function and then returned to a new memory location which will have whatever the required alignment of the output type is.

[§](https://docs.rs#failure)Failure

- If the types don’t have the same size this fails to compile.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
// compiles:
let bytes: [u8; 2] = bytemuck::must_cast(12_u16);
```

---

# must_cast_mut in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.must_cast_mut.html

`pub const fn must_cast_mut<A: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) + [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html), B: [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) + [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(
    a: [&mut A](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [&mut B](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)Available on

**crate feature**only.`must_cast`## Expand description

Convert a `&mut A` into `&mut B` if infalliable, or fail to compile.

As [ must_cast_ref](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html), but

`mut`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let mut i = 12_u16;
// compiles:
let bytes: &mut [u8; 2] = bytemuck::must_cast_mut(&mut i);
```

---

# must_cast_ref in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.must_cast_ref.html

# Function must_cast_ref

[Source](../src/bytemuck/must.rs.html#67-71) `pub const fn must_cast_ref<A: `[NoUninit](trait.NoUninit.html), B: [AnyBitPattern](trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(a: [&A](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [&B](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)

Available on **crate feature **`must_cast` only.

## Expand description

Convert `&A` into `&B` if infalliable, or fail to compile.

[§](#failure)Failure

- If the target type has a greater alignment requirement.
- If the source type and target type aren’t the same size.

[§](#examples)Examples

`let bytes: &[u8; 2] = bytemuck::must_cast_ref(&12_u16);`

[ⓘ](#)`let bytes : &[u8; 3] = bytemuck::must_cast_ref(&12_u16);`

[ⓘ](#)`let bytes : &u16 = bytemuck::must_cast_ref(&[1u8, 2u8]);`

---

# must_cast_slice in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.must_cast_slice.html

`pub const fn must_cast_slice<A: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html), B: [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(a: &[[A]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)) -> &[[B]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)Available on

**crate feature**only.`must_cast`## Expand description

Convert `&[A]` into `&[B]` (possibly with a change in length) if
infalliable, or fail to compile.

- `input.as_ptr() as usize == output.as_ptr() as usize`
- `input.len() * size_of::<A>() == output.len() * size_of::<B>()`

[§](https://docs.rs#failure)Failure

- If the target type has a greater alignment requirement.
- If the target element type doesn’t evenly fit into the current element
type (eg: 3 `u16`values is 1.5`u32`values, so that’s a failure).
- Similarly, you can’t convert from a non-[ZST](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/exotic-sizes.html#zero-sized-types-zsts)to a ZST (e.g. 3`u8`values is not any number of`()`values).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let indicies: &[u16] = &[1, 2, 3];
// compiles:
let bytes: &[u8] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice(indicies);
```
```
let zsts: &[()] = &[(), (), ()];
// compiles:
let bytes: &[u8] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice(zsts);
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// fails to compile (bytes.len() might not be a multiple of 2):
let byte_pairs : &[[u8; 2]] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice(bytes);
```

---

# must_cast_slice_mut in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html

`pub const fn must_cast_slice_mut<A: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) + [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html), B: [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) + [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(
    a: &mut [[A]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html),
) -> &mut [[B]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html)Available on

**crate feature**only.`must_cast`## Expand description

Convert `&mut [A]` into `&mut [B]` (possibly with a change in length) if
infalliable, or fail to compile.

As [ must_cast_slice](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice.html), but

`&mut`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let mut indicies = [1, 2, 3];
let indicies: &mut [u16] = &mut indicies;
// compiles:
let bytes: &mut [u8] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice_mut(indicies);
```
```
let zsts: &mut [()] = &mut [(), (), ()];
// compiles:
let bytes: &mut [u8] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice_mut(zsts);
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// fails to compile (bytes.len() might not be a multiple of 2):
let byte_pairs : &mut [[u8; 2]] = bytemuck::must_cast_slice_mut(bytes);
```

`pub fn try_cast_slice<A: `[NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html), B: [AnyBitPattern](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)>(
    a: &[[A]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<&[[B]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html), [PodCastError](https://docs.rs/enum.PodCastError.html)>## Expand description

Try to convert `&[A]` into `&[B]` (possibly with a change in length).

- `input.as_ptr() as usize == output.as_ptr() as usize`
- `input.len() * size_of::<A>() == output.len() * size_of::<B>()`

[§](https://docs.rs#failure)Failure

- If the target type has a greater alignment requirement and the input slice isn’t aligned.
- If the target element type is a different size from the current element
type, and the output slice wouldn’t be a whole number of elements when
accounting for the size change (eg: 3 `u16`values is 1.5`u32`values, so that’s a failure).
- Similarly, you can’t convert between a [ZST](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/exotic-sizes.html#zero-sized-types-zsts)and a non-ZST.

---

# write_zeroes in bytemuck - Rust

## Expand description

Fill all bytes of `target` with zeroes (see [ Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)).

This is similar to `*target = Zeroable::zeroed()`, but guarantees that any
padding bytes in `target` are zeroed as well.

See also [ fill_zeroes](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_zeroes.html), if you have a slice rather than a single value.

# ByteEq in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.ByteEq.html

`#[derive(ByteEq)]`**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `PartialEq` and `Eq` trait for a type

The macro implements `PartialEq` and `Eq` by casting both sides of the
comparison to a byte slice and then compares those.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

Since this implements a byte wise comparison, the behavior of floating point
numbers does not match their usual comparison behavior. Additionally other
custom comparison behaviors of the individual fields are also ignored. This
also does not implement `StructuralPartialEq` / `StructuralEq` like
`PartialEq` / `Eq` would. This means you can’t pattern match on the values.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, NoUninit, ByteEq)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Test {
  a: u32,
  b: char,
  c: f32,
}
```
```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, ByteEq)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Test<const N: usize> {
  a: [u32; N],
}
unsafe impl<const N: usize> NoUninit for Test<N> {}
```

---

The macro implements `Hash` by casting the value to a byte slice and hashing

# CheckedBitPattern in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.CheckedBitPattern.html

`#[derive(CheckedBitPattern)]`**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `CheckedBitPattern` trait for a struct or enum.

The macro ensures that the type follows all the the safety requirements
for the `CheckedBitPattern` trait and derives the required `Bits` type
definition and `is_valid_bit_pattern` method for the type automatically.

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed:

If applied to a struct:

- All fields must implement `CheckedBitPattern`
- The struct must be `#[repr(C)]`or`#[repr(transparent)]`
- The struct must contain no generic parameters

If applied to an enum:

- The enum must be explicit `#[repr(Int)]`
- All fields in variants must implement `CheckedBitPattern`
- The enum must contain no generic parameters

**crate feature**only.`derive`## Expand description

# NoUninit in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.NoUninit.html

```
#[derive(NoUninit)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[bytemuck]
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `NoUninit` trait for a struct or enum

The macro ensures that the type follows all the the safety requirements
for the `NoUninit` trait.

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed
(the rest of the constraints are guaranteed by the `NoUninit` subtrait
bounds, i.e. the type must be `Sized + Copy + 'static`):

If applied to a struct:

- All fields in the struct must implement `NoUninit`
- The struct must be `#[repr(C)]`or`#[repr(transparent)]`
- The struct must not contain any padding bytes
- The struct must contain no generic parameters

If applied to an enum:

- The enum must be explicit `#[repr(Int)]`,`#[repr(C)]`, or both
- If the enum has fields:
- All fields must implement `NoUninit`
- All variants must not contain any padding bytes
- All variants must be of the the same size
- There must be no padding bytes between the discriminant and any of the variant fields

- All fields must implement
- The enum must contain no generic parameters

# Pod in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.Pod.html

```
#[derive(Pod)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[bytemuck]
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `Pod` trait for a struct

The macro ensures that the struct follows all the the safety requirements
for the `Pod` trait.

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed

- All fields in the struct must implement `Pod`
- The struct must be `#[repr(C)]`or`#[repr(transparent)]`
- The struct must not contain any padding bytes
- The struct contains no generic parameters, if it is not
`#[repr(transparent)]`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Pod, Zeroable)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Test {
  a: u16,
  b: u16,
}
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Pod, Zeroable)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Generic<A, B> {
  a: A,
  b: PhantomData<B>,
}
```
If the struct is generic, it must be `#[repr(transparent)]` also.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Pod, Zeroable)]
#[repr(C)] // must be `#[repr(transparent)]`
struct Generic<A> {
  a: A,
}
```
If the struct is generic and `#[repr(transparent)]`, then it is only `Pod`
when all of its generics are `Pod`, not just its fields.

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Pod, Zeroable)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Generic<A, B> {
  a: A,
  b: PhantomData<B>,
}
let _: u32 = bytemuck::cast(Generic { a: 4u32, b: PhantomData::<u32> });
```

# TransparentWrapper in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.TransparentWrapper.html

```
#[derive(TransparentWrapper)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[bytemuck]
    #[transparent]
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `TransparentWrapper` trait for a struct

The macro ensures that the struct follows all the the safety requirements
for the `TransparentWrapper` trait.

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed

- The struct must be `#[repr(transparent)]`
- The struct must contain the `Wrapped`type
- Any ZST fields must be `Zeroable`

If the struct only contains a single field, the `Wrapped` type will
automatically be determined. If there is more then one field in the struct,
you need to specify the `Wrapped` type using `#[transparent(T)]`. Due to
technical limitations, the type in the `#[transparent(Type)]` needs to be
the exact same token sequence as the corresponding type in the struct
definition.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, TransparentWrapper)]
#[repr(transparent)]
#[transparent(u16)]
struct Test<T> {
  inner: u16,
  extra: PhantomData<T>,
}
```
If the struct contains more than one field, the `Wrapped` type must be
explicitly specified.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, TransparentWrapper)]
#[repr(transparent)]
// missing `#[transparent(u16)]`
struct Test<T> {
  inner: u16,
  extra: PhantomData<T>,
}
```
Any ZST fields must be `Zeroable`.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
struct NonTransparentSafeZST;
#[derive(TransparentWrapper)]
#[repr(transparent)]
#[transparent(u16)]
struct Test<T> {
  inner: u16,
  extra: PhantomData<T>,
  another_extra: NonTransparentSafeZST, // not `Zeroable`
}
```

# Zeroable in bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.0/derive.Zeroable.html

```
#[derive(Zeroable)]
{
    // Attributes available to this derive:
    #[bytemuck]
    #[zeroable]
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`derive`## Expand description

Derive the `Zeroable` trait for a type.

The macro ensures that the type follows all the the safety requirements
for the `Zeroable` trait.

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed on a struct:

- All fields in the struct must implement `Zeroable`

The following constraints need to be satisfied for the macro to succeed on an enum:

- The enum has an explicit `#[repr(Int)]`,`#[repr(C)]`, or`#[repr(C, Int)]`.
- The enum has a variant with discriminant 0 (explicitly or implicitly).
- All fields in the variant with discriminant 0 (if any) must implement
`Zeroable`

The macro always succeeds on unions.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroable)]
#[repr(C)]
struct Test {
  a: u16,
  b: u16,
}
```
```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroable)]
#[repr(i32)]
enum Values {
  A = 0,
  B = 1,
  C = 2,
}
#[derive(Clone, Zeroable)]
#[repr(C)]
enum Implicit {
  A(bool, u8, char),
  B(String),
  C(std::num::NonZeroU8),
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-bounds)Custom bounds

Custom bounds for the derived `Zeroable` impl can be given using the
`#[zeroable(bound = "")]` helper attribute.

Using this attribute additionally opts-in to “perfect derive” semantics, where instead of adding bounds for each generic type parameter, bounds are added for each field’s type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
#[derive(Clone, Zeroable)]
#[zeroable(bound = "")]
struct AlwaysZeroable<T> {
  a: PhantomData<T>,
}
AlwaysZeroable::<std::num::NonZeroU8>::zeroed();
```
```
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroable)]
#[repr(u8)]
#[zeroable(bound = "")]
enum MyOption<T> {
  None,
  Some(T),
}
assert!(matches!(MyOption::<std::num::NonZeroU8>::zeroed(), MyOption::None));
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone, Zeroable)]
#[zeroable(bound = "T: Copy")]
struct ZeroableWhenTIsCopy<T> {
  a: PhantomData<T>,
}
ZeroableWhenTIsCopy::<String>::zeroed();
```
The restriction that all fields must be Zeroable is still applied, and this is enforced using the mentioned “perfect derive” semantics.

```
#[derive(Clone, Zeroable)]
#[zeroable(bound = "")]
struct ZeroableWhenTIsZeroable<T> {
  a: T,
}
ZeroableWhenTIsZeroable::<u32>::zeroed();
```

---

# rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/latest/target-redirect/rapid_qoi/index.html

## Expand description

QOI - The “Quite OK Image” format for fast, lossless image compression

QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and 20% better compression.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-format)Data Format

A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data “chunks” and an 8-byte end marker.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct QoiHeader {
    magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
    width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
    height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
    channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
    colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
}
```
Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.

Pixels are encoded as

- a run of the previous pixel
- an index into an array of previously seen pixels
- a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
- full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values

The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel (“un-premultiplied alpha”).

A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.

The hash function for the index is:

Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.

The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
presence of an 8-bit tag first.

The byte stream’s end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
The possible chunks are:

```
.- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  0  0 |     index       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b00`

6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`

A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.

```
.- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----+-----+-----|
|  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b01`

2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`

The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
`0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
|  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
`---------------------------------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b10`

6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`

4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`

The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
```
The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.

Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
|         Byte[0]         |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
|-------+-----------------|
|  1  1 |       run       |
`-------------------------`
```
2-bit tag `0b11`

6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`

The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
(`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
`QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
`-------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111110`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.

```
.- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
|         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
|  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
|-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
|  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
`-----------------------------------------------------------------`
```
8-bit tag `0b11111111`

8-bit   red channel value

8-bit green channel value

8-bit  blue channel value

8-bit alpha channel value

[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! <https://phoboslab.org>
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! QOI encodes and decodes images in a lossless format. Compared to stb_image and
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! stb_image_write QOI offers 20x-50x faster encoding, 3x-4x faster decoding and
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! 20% better compression.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! # Data Format
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! A QOI file has a 14 byte header, followed by any number of data "chunks" and an
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! 8-byte end marker.
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! ```rust
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! #[repr(C)]
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! struct QoiHeader {
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!     magic: [u8; 4], // magic bytes "qoif"
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!     width: u32,     // image width in pixels (BE)
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     height: u32,    // image height in pixels (BE)
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     channels: u8,   // 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     colorspace: u8, // 0 = sRGB with linear alpha, 1 = all channels linear
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! }
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ```
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! Images are encoded from top to bottom, left to right. The decoder and encoder
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! start with `{r: 0, g: 0, b: 0, a: 255}` as the previous pixel value. An image is
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! complete when all pixels specified by width * height have been covered.\
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! Pixels are encoded as
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!  * a run of the previous pixel
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!  * an index into an array of previously seen pixels
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!  * a difference to the previous pixel value in r,g,b
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!  * full r,g,b or r,g,b,a values
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! The color channels are assumed to not be premultiplied with the alpha channel
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ("un-premultiplied alpha").
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! A running `array: [u32; 64]` (zero-initialized) of previously seen pixel values is
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! maintained by the encoder and decoder. Each pixel that is seen by the encoder
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! and decoder is put into this array at the position formed by a hash function of
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! the color value. In the encoder, if the pixel value at the index matches the
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! current pixel, this index position is written to the stream as QOI_OP_INDEX.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! The hash function for the index is:
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! ```rust,ignore
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! index_position = (r * 3 + g * 5 + b * 7 + a * 11) % 64
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ```
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! Each chunk starts with a 2- or 8-bit tag, followed by a number of data bits. The
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! bit length of chunks is divisible by 8 - i.e. all chunks are byte aligned. All
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! values encoded in these data bits have the most significant bit on the left.\
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! The 8-bit tags have precedence over the 2-bit tags. A decoder must check for the
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! presence of an 8-bit tag first.
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! The byte stream's end is marked with 7 `0x00` bytes followed a single `0x01` byte.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! The possible chunks are:
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! ```text
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! .- QOI_OP_INDEX ----------.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! |-------+-----------------|
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! |  0  0 |     index       |
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! `-------------------------`
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! 2-bit tag `0b00`\
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! 6-bit index into the color index array: `0..=63`\
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! A valid encoder must not issue 7 or more consecutive `QOI_OP_INDEX` chunks to the
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! index 0, to avoid confusion with the 8 byte end marker.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! ```text
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! .- QOI_OP_DIFF -----------.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! |-------+-----+-----+-----|
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! |  0  1 |  dr |  dg |  db |
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! `-------------------------`
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! ```
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! 2-bit tag `0b01`\
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! 2-bit   red channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! 2-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! 2-bit  blue channel difference from the previous pixel between `-2..=1`\
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! so `1 - 2` will result in `255`, while `255 + 1` will result in `0`.\
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 2. E.g. `-2` is stored as
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! `0` (`0b00`). `1` is stored as `3` (`0b11`).\
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```text
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! .- QOI_OP_LUMA -------------------------------------.
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! |         Byte[0]         |         Byte[1]         |
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! |-------+-----------------+-------------+-----------|
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! |  1  0 |  green diff     |   dr - dg   |  db - dg  |
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! `---------------------------------------------------`
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! 2-bit tag `0b10`\
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! 6-bit green channel difference from the previous pixel `-32..=31`\
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! 4-bit   red channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`\
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! 4-bit  blue channel difference minus green channel difference `-8..=7`\
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! The green channel is used to indicate the general direction of change and is
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! encoded in 6 bits. The red and blue channels (dr and db) base their diffs off
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! of the green channel difference and are encoded in 4 bits. I.e.:
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! ```rust,ignore
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! dr_dg = (last_px.r - cur_px.r) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! db_dg = (last_px.b - cur_px.b) - (last_px.g - cur_px.g)
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! The difference to the current channel values are using a wraparound operation,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! so `10 - 13` will result in `253`, while `250 + 7` will result in `1`.\
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! Values are stored as unsigned integers with a bias of 32 for the green channel
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! and a bias of 8 for the red and blue channel.\
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```text
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! .- QOI_OP_RUN ------------.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! |         Byte[0]         |
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 |
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! |-------+-----------------|
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! |  1  1 |       run       |
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! `-------------------------`
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! 2-bit tag `0b11`\
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! 6-bit run-length repeating the previous pixel: `1..=62`\
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! The run-length is stored with a bias of -1. Note that the run-lengths 63 and 64
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! (`0b111110` and `0b111111`) are illegal as they are occupied by the `QOI_OP_RGB` and
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! `QOI_OP_RGBA` tags.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! ```text
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! .- QOI_OP_RGB ------------------------------------------.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! |         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] |
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! |-------------------------+---------+---------+---------|
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! |  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  0 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! `-------------------------------------------------------`
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! 8-bit tag `0b11111110`\
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! 8-bit   red channel value\
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! 8-bit green channel value\
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! 8-bit  blue channel value\
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! The alpha value remains unchanged from the previous pixel.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! ```text
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! .- QOI_OP_RGBA ---------------------------------------------------.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! |         Byte[0]         | Byte[1] | Byte[2] | Byte[3] | Byte[4] |
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! |  7  6  5  4  3  2  1  0 | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  | 7 .. 0  |
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! |-------------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------|
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! |  1  1  1  1  1  1  1  1 |   red   |  green  |  blue   |  alpha  |
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! `-----------------------------------------------------------------`
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ```
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! 8-bit tag `0b11111111`\
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! 8-bit   red channel value\
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! 8-bit green channel value\
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! 8-bit  blue channel value\
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! 8-bit alpha channel value
[147](https://docs.rs#147)#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)#![deny(missing_copy_implementations)]
[149](https://docs.rs#149)#![deny(missing_debug_implementations)]
[150](https://docs.rs#150)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[151](https://docs.rs#151)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[153](https://docs.rs#153)extern crate alloc;
[154](https://docs.rs#154)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)use core::{
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    convert::TryInto,
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    fmt::{self, Display},
[158](https://docs.rs#158)};
[159](https://docs.rs#159)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)mod decode;
[161](https://docs.rs#161)mod encode;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)pub use decode::DecodeError;
[164](https://docs.rs#164)pub use encode::EncodeError;
[165](https://docs.rs#165)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)const QOI_OP_INDEX: u8 = 0x00; /* 00xxxxxx */
[167](https://docs.rs#167)const QOI_OP_DIFF: u8 = 0x40; /* 01xxxxxx */
[168](https://docs.rs#168)const QOI_OP_LUMA: u8 = 0x80; /* 10xxxxxx */
[169](https://docs.rs#169)const QOI_OP_RUN: u8 = 0xc0; /* 11xxxxxx */
[170](https://docs.rs#170)const QOI_OP_RGB: u8 = 0xfe; /* 11111110 */
[171](https://docs.rs#171)const QOI_OP_RGBA: u8 = 0xff; /* 11111111 */
[172](https://docs.rs#172)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)const QOI_MAGIC: u32 = u32::from_be_bytes(*b"qoif");
[174](https://docs.rs#174)const QOI_HEADER_SIZE: usize = 14;
[175](https://docs.rs#175)const QOI_PADDING: usize = 8;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// Trait for pixel types.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// Supports byte operations, channels accessing and modifying.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)pub trait Pixel: Copy + Eq {
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    fn new() -> Self;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    fn new_opaque() -> Self;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    fn read(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]);
[187](https://docs.rs#187)
[188](https://docs.rs#188)    fn write(&self, bytes: &mut [u8]);
[189](https://docs.rs#189)
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var;
[191](https://docs.rs#191)
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    fn rgb(&self) -> [u8; 3];
[193](https://docs.rs#193)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    fn rgba(&self) -> [u8; 4];
[195](https://docs.rs#195)
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    fn r(&self) -> u8;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    fn g(&self) -> u8;
[199](https://docs.rs#199)
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    fn b(&self) -> u8;
[201](https://docs.rs#201)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    fn a(&self) -> u8;
[203](https://docs.rs#203)
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn set_r(&mut self, r: u8);
[205](https://docs.rs#205)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    fn set_g(&mut self, g: u8);
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    fn set_b(&mut self, b: u8);
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    fn set_a(&mut self, a: u8);
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    fn set_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8);
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    fn set_rgba(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8, a: u8);
[215](https://docs.rs#215)
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    fn add_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8);
[217](https://docs.rs#217)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    fn hash(&self) -> u8;
[219](https://docs.rs#219)}
[220](https://docs.rs#220)
[221](https://docs.rs#221)impl Pixel for [u8; 3] {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool = false;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    #[inline]
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    fn new() -> Self {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        [0; 3]
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    #[inline]
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    fn new_opaque() -> Self {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        [0; 3]
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    #[inline]
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    fn read(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) {
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        self.copy_from_slice(bytes);
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    #[inline]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    fn write(&self, bytes: &mut [u8]) {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        assert_eq!(bytes.len(), self.len());
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        bytes.copy_from_slice(self)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    #[inline]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var {
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        let r = self[0].wrapping_sub(prev[0]);
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let g = self[1].wrapping_sub(prev[1]);
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        let b = self[2].wrapping_sub(prev[2]);
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        Var { r, g, b }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    }
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    #[inline]
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    fn r(&self) -> u8 {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        self[0]
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    }
[258](https://docs.rs#258)
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    #[inline]
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    fn g(&self) -> u8 {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        self[1]
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    #[inline]
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    fn b(&self) -> u8 {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        self[2]
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    }
[268](https://docs.rs#268)
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    #[inline]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    fn rgb(&self) -> [u8; 3] {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        *self
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    }
[273](https://docs.rs#273)
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    #[inline]
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    fn rgba(&self) -> [u8; 4] {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        unreachable!()
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    }
[278](https://docs.rs#278)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    #[inline]
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    fn a(&self) -> u8 {
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        255
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    #[inline]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    fn set_r(&mut self, r: u8) {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        self[0] = r;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    #[inline]
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    fn set_g(&mut self, g: u8) {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        self[1] = g;
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    #[inline]
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    fn set_b(&mut self, b: u8) {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        self[2] = b;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    }
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    #[inline]
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    fn set_a(&mut self, a: u8) {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        debug_assert_eq!(a, 255);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    #[inline]
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    fn set_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        self[0] = r;
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        self[1] = g;
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        self[2] = b;
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    #[inline]
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    fn set_rgba(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8, a: u8) {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        debug_assert_eq!(a, 255);
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        self[0] = r;
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        self[1] = g;
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        self[2] = b;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    #[inline]
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    fn add_rgb(&mut self, r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        self[0] = self[0].wrapping_add(r);
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        self[1] = self[1].wrapping_add(g);
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        self[2] = self[2].wrapping_add(b);
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    // #[inline]
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    // fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    //     let [r, g, b] = self;
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    //     r.wrapping_mul(3)
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    //         .wrapping_add(g.wrapping_mul(5))
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    //         .wrapping_add(b.wrapping_mul(7).wrapping_add(245))
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    //         & 63
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    // }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    #[inline]
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[338](https://docs.rs#338)        let [r, g, b] = *self;
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        let v = u32::from_ne_bytes([r, g, b, 0xff]);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        let s = (((v as u64) << 32) | (v as u64)) & 0xFF00FF0000FF00FF;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        s.wrapping_mul(0x030007000005000Bu64.to_le()).swap_bytes() as u8 & 63
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    }
[344](https://docs.rs#344)}
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)// /// Four channel pixel type.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)// /// Typically channels are Red, Green, Blue and Alpha.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)// #[repr(transparent)]
[349](https://docs.rs#349)// #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)// pub struct Rgba {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//     pub rgba: [u8; 4],
[352](https://docs.rs#352)// }
[353](https://docs.rs#353)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)impl Pixel for [u8; 4] {
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    const HAS_ALPHA: bool = true;
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    #[inline]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)    fn new() -> Self {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        [0; 4]

[384](https://docs.rs#384)    fn var(&self, prev: &Self) -> Var {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        let [r, g, b, a] = *self;
[386](https://docs.rs#386)        let [pr, pg, pb, pa] = *prev;
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        debug_assert_eq!(a, pa);
[388](https://docs.rs#388)
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        let r = r.wrapping_sub(pr);
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        let g = g.wrapping_sub(pg);
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        let b = b.wrapping_sub(pb);
[392](https://docs.rs#392)

[474](https://docs.rs#474)    fn hash(&self) -> u8 {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        let v = u32::from_ne_bytes(*self);
[476](https://docs.rs#476)        let s = (((v as u64) << 32) | (v as u64)) & 0xFF00FF0000FF00FF;
[477](https://docs.rs#477)
[478](https://docs.rs#478)        s.wrapping_mul(0x030007000005000Bu64.to_le()).swap_bytes() as u8 & 63
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    }

[481](https://docs.rs#481)
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// Color variance value.
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// Wrapping difference between two pixels.
[484](https://docs.rs#484)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
[485](https://docs.rs#485)#[repr(C)]
[486](https://docs.rs#486)pub struct Var {
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    pub r: u8,
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    pub g: u8,
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    pub b: u8,
[490](https://docs.rs#490)}
[491](https://docs.rs#491)
[492](https://docs.rs#492)impl Var {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    #[inline]
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    fn diff(&self) -> Option<u8> {
[495](https://docs.rs#495)        let r = self.r.wrapping_add(2);
[496](https://docs.rs#496)        let g = self.g.wrapping_add(2);
[497](https://docs.rs#497)        let b = self.b.wrapping_add(2);
[498](https://docs.rs#498)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        match r | g | b {
[500](https://docs.rs#500)            0x00..=0x03 => Some(QOI_OP_DIFF | (r << 4) as u8 | (g << 2) as u8 | b as u8),
[501](https://docs.rs#501)            _ => None,
[502](https://docs.rs#502)        }
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    }
[504](https://docs.rs#504)
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    #[inline]
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    fn luma(&self) -> Option<[u8; 2]> {
[507](https://docs.rs#507)        let r = self.r.wrapping_add(8).wrapping_sub(self.g);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        let g = self.g.wrapping_add(32);
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        let b = self.b.wrapping_add(8).wrapping_sub(self.g);
[510](https://docs.rs#510)
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        match (r | b, g) {
[512](https://docs.rs#512)            (0x00..=0x0F, 0x00..=0x3F) => Some([QOI_OP_LUMA | g, r << 4 | b]),
[513](https://docs.rs#513)            _ => None,
[514](https://docs.rs#514)        }
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    }
[516](https://docs.rs#516)}

# Qoi in rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/latest/target-redirect/rapid_qoi/struct.Qoi.html

## Expand description

QOI descriptor value.

This value is parsed from image header during decoding.

Or provided by caller to drive encoding.

Decode a QOI image from bytes slice.

Decoded raw RGB or RGBA pixels are written into `output` slice.

On success this function returns `Ok(qoi)` with `qoi` describing image dimensions and color space.

On failure this function returns `Err(err)` with `err` describing cause of the error.

Decode a QOI image from bytes slice.

`bytes` does not include QOI header. Uses provided `Qoi` value instead.

Decoded raw RGB or RGBA (depending on `self.colors` value) pixels are written into `output` slice.

On success this function returns `Ok(())`.

On failure this function returns `Err(err)` with `err` describing cause of the error.

Decode a QOI image from bytes slice.

Decoded raw RGB or RGBA pixels are written into allocated `Vec`.

# Enum Colors

[Source](../src/rapid_qoi/lib.rs.html#520-532) ```
pub enum Colors {
    Srgb,

    Rgb,

# DecodeError in rapid_qoi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rapid-qoi/latest/target-redirect/rapid_qoi/enum.DecodeError.html

```
pub enum DecodeError {
    NotEnoughData,
    InvalidMagic,
    InvalidChannelsValue,
    InvalidColorSpaceValue,
    OutputIsTooSmall,
}
```
## Expand description

Errros that may occur during image decoding.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NotEnoughData)

### NotEnoughData

Buffer does not contain enough encoded data.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidMagic)

### InvalidMagic

Encoded header contains invalid magic value.

First four bytes must contain `b"qoif"`.

This usually indicates that buffer does not contain QOI image.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidChannelsValue)

### InvalidChannelsValue

Encoded header contains invalud channels number.

QOI supports only images with `3` or `4` channels.

Any other value cannot be produced by valid encoder.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.InvalidColorSpaceValue)

### InvalidColorSpaceValue

Encoded header contains invalud color space value.’
QOI supports only images with SRGB color channels and linear alpha (if present) denoted by `0` and all linear channels denoted by `1`.

Any other value cannot be produced by valid encoder.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.OutputIsTooSmall)

### OutputIsTooSmall

Output buffer is too small to fit decoded image.

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [arg](https://docs.rs/macro.arg.html)
- Create an `Arg`
- [command](https://docs.rs/macro.command.html)- `cargo`
- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_authors.html)- authors - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at
compile time in the form:
`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_description.html)- description - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_version.html)- version - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- [value_](https://docs.rs/macro.value_parser.html)- parser
- Select a `ValueParser`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.

- Specifies a logical group of [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- [ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgMatches.html)
- Container for parse results.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- Build a command-line interface.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgAction](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgAction.html)
- Behavior of arguments when they are encountered while parsing
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- Represents the color preferences for program output

- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.

- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap::Command

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

Options:
